You compare things and places (plus… que, moins… que, aussi… que) and say which is “the most”.
This flat is bigger than the other one.
It’s cheaper, but it’s also further away.
It’s the most beautiful flat in the neighbourhood.
This coffee is better than the other one.
To compare with plus… que, moins… que, aussi… que.
To use the superlative: le plus grand, la moins chère.
To use the irregular forms: meilleur, mieux, pire.
To compare with verbs and nouns too: il travaille plus que moi, plus de place.
To talk about a home: rent, floor, lift, light.
March. Ioana and Julien have decided to move in together. On Saturday they saw two flats. In the evening, at a café, they compare them.
So, which one do you prefer? The one in Croix-Rousse or the one in Monplaisir?
It’s hard! The Croix-Rousse flat is prettier. It’s brighter and the view is magnificent.
Yes, but it’s on the fifth floor with no lift! And it’s smaller: sixty square metres.
The Monplaisir one is eighty square metres. It’s bigger and more modern. But it has less charm.
And the rent? In Croix-Rousse it’s nine hundred and fifty euros. In Monplaisir, eleven hundred.
So Croix-Rousse is cheaper. But Monplaisir is closer to your school.
True. And your office is as far from both flats. Twenty minutes by metro.
There’s one important thing: the piano. Which flat has more room for a piano?
A piano? You want to buy a piano?
Not me… But I think you play better on a real piano than on your little electric keyboard!
Ha ha! Then Monplaisir. The living room is the bigger of the two. And it’s the quietest neighbourhood.
But no view… and Sophie’s bakery is further away. Her croissants are the best in Lyon!
Listen, the best solution is to make a list. The pros and cons of each flat.
OK. But one thing is sure: with you, any flat will be the most beautiful in the world.
PLUS has three pronunciations! “plu” in comparisons before a consonant (plus grand), “pluz” before a vowel (plus intéressant), and “plus” at the end or when it means “more” (j’en veux plus).
Meilleur = “may-YUR”. Careful: “ill” after “e” is read “y”, as in “famille”.
Mieux = “myuh”. As in “tant mieux” (so much the better).
“Le plus bel appartement” = “luh plu bel a-par-tuh-MÃ”: before a vowel, “beau” becomes “bel”, which sounds like the feminine “belle”.
Mètre carré = “metr ka-RAY”. Written m² and read “mètres carrés”.
French compares with three degrees, just like English:
Il est plus grand que l’autre.
It’s bigger than the other one.
Il est moins cher que l’autre.
It’s less expensive than the other one.
Il est aussi loin que l’autre.
It’s as far as the other one.
The adjective agrees as usual: “La cuisine est plus grande que le salon” (grande, feminine). And after “que” you use the stressed pronouns: plus grand que moi, que toi, que lui, qu’elle.
“Que” becomes “qu’” before a vowel: “plus petit qu’elle”, “aussi beau qu’avant”.

“In” after a superlative is “de”: “le plus beau du monde” (the most beautiful in the world), “la meilleure de Lyon”. Not “dans le monde”.
3. The irregular forms: meilleur, mieux, pire
Like English (“good → better”, “well → better”), French has special forms. This is where the biggest trap is:
This croissant is better. (bon → adjective, about a thing)
You play the piano better. (bien → adverb, about an action)
It’s the worst winter in ten years.
Never “plus bon” or “plus bien”! The classic mistake: “C’est plus bon” → correct: “C’est meilleur”. And “Il parle plus bien” → correct: “Il parle mieux”.
Tip: English uses “better” for both, so ask yourself: is it about a thing (good → meilleur) or an action (well → mieux)?
You can also compare verbs (plus / moins / autant after the verb) and nouns (plus de / moins de / autant de):
plus de / moins de / autant de + noun + que
Il y a plus de place à Monplaisir.
I have as many books as you.
I eat less meat than before.
With adjectives: aussi (aussi grand). With verbs and nouns: autant (autant de place, il travaille autant). Not “aussi de”.
on the ground floor / on the fifth floor
to move in / to move out

On Sunday evening Ioana and Julien sat down at the kitchen table with a big sheet of paper and two pens: a red one and a green one.
In green they wrote the pros. In red, the cons. It was Julien’s idea. He’s more organised than Ioana.
For Croix-Rousse the green column was the longest: the view, the light, the charm, the price, Sophie’s bakery, the little restaurants.
In the red column there were only two things. But they were important: five floors with no lift, and no room for a piano.
For Monplaisir it was the opposite. More space, more comfort, a lift, parking. But the flat was more expensive and the neighbourhood less lively.
“The problem,” said Julien, “is that Croix-Rousse is the best flat for you, and Monplaisir the best for me.”
Ioana thought about it. “No. The best flat is the one where we’re both happy.”
The next day they phoned the agency to ask the Croix-Rousse landlord a question.
And then, surprise! The landlord had a second flat in the same building, on the first floor. It was a little bigger, and it had a small courtyard.
It was less bright than the other one, it’s true. The view was less beautiful. But there was enough room for a piano, and Sophie’s bakery was right opposite.
They viewed it on Tuesday. On Wednesday they signed the lease.
On Thursday Julien found an old second-hand piano online. It was cheaper than a bike!
On Friday Sophie heard the news. She cried out with joy: “My best customers are becoming my neighbours! Free croissants on the first day!”
And Madame Bernard? She was a little sad. “The first floor is far from me…” But the building was in the same street. As for Victor, he had already found the way.
Le propriétaire avait un autre appartement dans le même immeuble
